The Siberian sturgeon Acipenser baerii is a large, long-lived freshwater fish native to the river systems of Siberia, with the Ob-Irtysh basin supporting one of its most well-studied populations. Field surveys from this region indicate that individuals attain a total length at puberty of approximately 106.5 cm [Lp = approximately 106.5 cm], a size that typically corresponds to the onset of gonadal maturation. The ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches 200 cm [Li = 200 cm], placing it among the larger members of the Acipenseridae family. Growth trajectories derived from mark-recapture studies reveal that females often achieve a greater ultimate wet weight than males, with the maximum recorded body mass in adults reaching 85,300 grams [Wwi = 85,300 grams], a figure consistent with the pronounced sexual size dimorphism observed across many sturgeon species. This substantial ultimate mass reflects decades of sustained somatic investment, during which individuals traverse a slow, steady growth curve before reaching their asymptotic dimensions late in life.

Early life stages of Acipenser baerii are characterized by a relatively rapid initial development, contingent upon thermal conditions during embryogenesis. Under a laboratory incubation regime held at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from fertilization to completion of yolk-sac larva emergence, is approximately 36 days [ab = approximately 36 days]. Newly emerged prolarvae possess a modest wet weight at birth of 0.0092 grams [Wwb = 0.0092 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter range of 2.37 to 2.92 mm. This lecithotrophic alevin then begins a crucial trophic switch to exogenous feeding as the yolk reserves are progressively depleted. The transition from yolk dependency to active feeding onset is a critical bottleneck; larvae that fail to initiate feeding within a narrow window soon after yolk absorption completion face starvation, underscoring the importance of synchronous prey availability in natural spawning grounds.

Sexual maturation in Siberian sturgeon proceeds at a deliberate pace, with puberty attained at a wet weight at puberty of roughly 9,000 grams [Wwp = roughly 9,000 grams] for individuals in the Ob-Irtysh basin. Data from this population indicate that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 10.5 years [tp = approximately 10.5 years], when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This age range of 9 to 12 years is typical for slow-maturing temperate acipenserids and reflects the substantial somatic growth required before reproductive activation. The onset of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis is triggered by a combination of size thresholds and seasonal environmental cues, with vitellogenesis initiating only after females have accumulated sufficient lipid reserves. Puberty is thus not strictly age-dependent but is instead modulated by individual growth rates, which in turn are influenced by prey density and thermal regime.

Reproductive effort in Acipenser baerii is characterized by an iteroparous, periodic spawning strategy, with individual females not spawning annually but rather at multi-year intervals. Under optimal conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the maximum reproductive rate, derived from the average fecundity of approximately 1,000,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,000,000 eggs per spawning event] combined with a spawning interval of roughly 2.7 years [F_R_i = a spawning interval of roughly 2.7 years], yields a substantial lifetime reproductive output. This high fecundity per event is typical of many potamodromous sturgeons and compensates for the low annual frequency of reproduction. The extended interval between spawnings allows females to rebuild the energetic reserves depleted during vitellogenesis and spawning migration. Broodstock held in aquaculture settings have been documented to produce clutches of similar magnitude, confirming the fecundity estimates obtained from wild-caught gravid females.

The species is renowned for its exceptional longevity, a life-history trait shared with other members of the Acipenseriformes. Maximum recorded longevity for Acipenser baerii in the Ob-Irtysh basin is approximately 63 years [am = approximately 63 years] for individuals living under thermal conditions averaging 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This extended lifespan allows for numerous reproductive opportunities across a mature female's life, despite the multi-year spawning interval. The combination of late puberty, large ultimate body size, and high fecundity per event positions the Siberian sturgeon as a classic K-selected strategist, with population dynamics heavily dependent on adult survival rather than juvenile recruitment. Conservation assessments for this species therefore emphasize the protection of large, old individuals, whose reproductive value far exceeds that of younger, smaller spawners. Understanding these demographic parameters is crucial for modeling population viability under current harvest and habitat fragmentation pressures.
